topics.title: Systems glossary
topics.summary: Systems terms with concrete chapter context.

cards.question: Contract — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The inputs, results, and rules that callers and implementations agree to.

cards.question: Layer — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A part of a system that performs one kind of work through a defined boundary.

cards.question: Value parameter — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A parameter object initialized from the argument; this vector has independent element storage.

cards.question: Reference parameter — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Another name for the caller’s object, with no new copy of that object.

cards.question: Mask — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A bit pattern selecting which bit positions an operation should affect.

cards.question: Bit field — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A fixed group of bits used to store one value within a larger word.

cards.question: Unsigned wrap — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Unsigned arithmetic reduces a result modulo one more than the type’s maximum value.

cards.question: Precondition — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A rule that must hold before an operation can safely perform its work.

cards.question: Rounding error — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The difference caused when an exact result must be stored as one of the available floating-point values.

cards.question: Relative tolerance — what does it mean?
cards.answer: An allowed error scaled to the magnitude of the compared values.

cards.question: Row-major layout — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Consecutive columns of one row occupy consecutive element positions.

cards.question: Alignment — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A rule about which addresses are valid starting points for an object type.

cards.question: Half-open range — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A range including its first position but excluding its end position.

cards.question: Iterator — what does it mean?
cards.answer: An object representing a position that a traversal can examine and advance.

cards.question: Object lifetime — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The interval during which a constructed object may be used according to its type’s rules.

cards.question: Ownership transfer — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Moving responsibility for releasing a resource from one owner to another.

cards.question: Size — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The number of live elements in a container.

cards.question: Capacity — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The number of elements that fit in currently reserved vector storage without reallocation.

cards.question: Fragmentation — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Space that exists but cannot be used for the desired request under an allocator’s rules.

cards.question: Commit point — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The operation at which a prepared change becomes the visible new state.

cards.question: Bounds error — what does it mean?
cards.answer: An access outside the valid element range of an object.

cards.question: Undefined behavior — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A program operation for which the C++ standard imposes no behavior requirements.

cards.question: Architectural state — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The registers and other state whose behavior an instruction set promises to software.

cards.question: Instruction set — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The operations and rules a machine exposes to programs.

cards.question: Subregister — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A named portion of a larger machine register.

cards.question: Zero extension — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Increasing a value’s width by filling the new high bits with zeros.

cards.question: Effective address — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The address value formed from the components of a machine addressing mode.

cards.question: Displacement — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A fixed offset included in an address calculation.

cards.question: Quotient — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The integer result of division after truncation toward zero in this C++ operation.

cards.question: Remainder — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The part left after multiplying the integer quotient by the divisor.

cards.question: Loop invariant — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A rule maintained before every repetition, used to explain the loop’s result.

cards.question: Control flow — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The order in which a program can execute its operations.

cards.question: ABI — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The binary-level agreement for calls, object layout, symbols, and other machine interfaces.

cards.question: Callee-saved register — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A register whose incoming value a callee must restore when required by the relevant ABI.

cards.question: Aliasing — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Two access paths referring to the same underlying object or storage.

cards.question: Observable behavior — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The effects that a valid optimization must preserve under the language’s rules.

cards.question: Privilege boundary — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A boundary across which code must have different authority to access resources.

cards.question: Validation — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Checking that a request satisfies its required shape, range, and permissions before acting on it.

cards.question: Fault — what does it mean?
cards.answer: An exception associated with an instruction that could not complete under the current conditions.

cards.question: Restart point — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The saved execution position used to retry an operation after a recoverable condition is repaired.

cards.question: Runnable — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Eligible to receive CPU time, though not necessarily executing now.

cards.question: State transition — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A permitted change from one named state to another after an event.

cards.question: Address space — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The mapping context in which a program interprets its virtual addresses.

cards.question: Backing storage — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The underlying storage reached through a mapping or handle.

cards.question: Page — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A fixed-size block in a virtual address space.

cards.question: Frame — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A fixed-size physical-memory block that can back a virtual page.

cards.question: Page-table entry — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A record containing mapping information and access-control state for a page.

cards.question: Protection fault — what does it mean?
cards.answer: An exception caused when an access violates the mapping’s permission rules.

cards.question: TLB — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A cache of recently used virtual-to-physical translations and related access information.

cards.question: Invalidation — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Removing a cached fact when the authoritative state no longer supports it.

cards.question: Copy on write — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Sharing unchanged backing and making a private copy before a permitted private mutation.

cards.question: Demand paging — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Providing backing for a permitted page when an access first requires it.

cards.question: Latency — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The elapsed delay for a particular operation or request.

cards.question: Bandwidth — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The amount of data that can be transferred per unit time under stated conditions.

cards.question: Spatial locality — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Using nearby locations within a short interval.

cards.question: Temporal locality — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Using the same location again before its useful cached state is displaced.

cards.question: Set associativity — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The number of entries in one cache set that can hold competing blocks.

cards.question: Tag — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The part of a block’s identity used to distinguish blocks selecting the same set.

cards.question: Cache hit — what does it mean?
cards.answer: An access whose required block is already present and usable at the modeled cache level.

cards.question: Conflict miss — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A repeated miss caused by restricted placement relative to the chosen fully associative reference model.

cards.question: Replacement policy — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The rule selecting which resident item to remove when space is needed.

cards.question: Dirty line — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A cached block containing changes that must be preserved before the block is discarded.

cards.question: Local miss rate — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Misses divided by requests reaching a particular cache level.

cards.question: AMAT — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Average memory-access time calculated under a stated cost model.

cards.question: File offset — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A byte position used to locate data in a file.

cards.question: Record boundary — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A division between logical items imposed by a format above the byte stream.

cards.question: File descriptor — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A process-local handle used to request operations on an open resource.

cards.question: Short transfer — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A successful operation that moves fewer bytes than requested.

cards.question: Buffering — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Temporarily collecting data so it can be passed onward in useful batches.

cards.question: Flush — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Requesting that buffered data move to the next layer defined by the API.

cards.question: Shared mapping — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A mapping whose writes affect the shared backing according to the mapping API’s rules.

cards.question: Private mapping — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A mapping whose private modifications do not become shared file changes under its contract.

cards.question: Open-file description — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Kernel-maintained state, such as a file offset, that multiple descriptors may reference.

cards.question: Fork — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A process-creation operation that creates a child with defined copies and shared references from its parent.

cards.question: Program image — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The executable code and associated user-space state installed in a process.

cards.question: Exec — what does it mean?
cards.answer: An operation that replaces the calling process’s program image rather than creating a second process.

cards.question: Reaping — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Collecting a terminated child’s status so its retained process record can be released.

cards.question: Exit status — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A result describing how a process terminated; its interpretation depends on the termination category.

cards.question: EOF — what does it mean?
cards.answer: End of stream: no more bytes will be delivered under the stream’s contract.

cards.question: Backpressure — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A limit that makes a producer wait or reduce output when a downstream consumer cannot keep up.

cards.question: Signal — what does it mean?
cards.answer: An asynchronous process notification with delivery and handling rules defined by the OS.

cards.question: Async-signal-safe — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Permitted for use in an asynchronous signal handler under the applicable API’s rules.

cards.question: Token — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A meaningful input unit such as a word or operator produced during parsing.

cards.question: Execution plan — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A validated description of the operations to perform before those operations are started.

cards.question: Interleaving — what does it mean?
cards.answer: One ordering of steps from activities whose lifetimes overlap.

cards.question: Concurrency — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Multiple activities in progress whose steps may be interleaved or run at the same time.

cards.question: Join — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Waiting for a thread’s completion and establishing the completion relationship needed to use its results.

cards.question: Partition — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A division of work into ranges or tasks with explicit coverage and overlap rules.

cards.question: Data race — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Conflicting concurrent C++ accesses, at least one a write, without the required atomicity or happens-before ordering.

cards.question: Logical race — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A result that depends on an undesired ordering of otherwise defined operations.

cards.question: Release/acquire — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A pair of atomic ordering operations that can establish visibility of preceding work when the acquire observes the release.

cards.question: Happens-before — what does it mean?
cards.answer: An ordering relation used by C++ to determine whether effects are properly ordered between evaluations.

cards.question: Critical section — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A region whose operations require coordinated access to shared state.

cards.question: Mutex — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A synchronization object that permits one cooperating owner at a time.

cards.question: Condition variable — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A waiting mechanism used with a mutex and a predicate over shared state.

cards.question: Spurious wakeup — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A return from waiting that does not itself prove the desired condition is true.

cards.question: Drain — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Consume already-accepted work before ending a closed queue or stream.

cards.question: Shutdown protocol — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The rules for stopping new work, waking waiters, finishing or discarding old work, and ending lifetimes.

cards.question: Deadlock — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A state in which participants cannot progress because each waits for conditions the waiting participants must supply.

cards.question: Circular wait — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A cycle of waiting dependencies, such as A waiting for B while B waits for A.

cards.question: Framing — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Rules that identify application message boundaries within a sequence of bytes.

cards.question: Byte stream — what does it mean?
cards.answer: An ordered sequence of bytes without a promise that transfer calls preserve message boundaries.

cards.question: Admission control — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A rule deciding whether new work can enter the system given current resource limits.

cards.question: Overload policy — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The chosen behavior when incoming work exceeds capacity, such as rejection, bounded waiting, or dropping.

cards.question: Readiness — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A notification that an I/O operation may be able to make progress under the API’s conditions.

cards.question: Would-block — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A nonblocking result indicating that immediate progress is unavailable without waiting.

cards.question: Throughput — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Completed work divided by the elapsed measurement interval.

cards.question: Percentile — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A position in an ordered sample or distribution, interpreted using a stated convention.

cards.question: Precomputation — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Doing reusable work once so later operations require less repeated effort.

cards.question: Complexity — what does it mean?
cards.answer: How a program’s required work or storage grows with input size.

cards.question: Amdahl’s law — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A time-based bound on whole-system speedup when only a stated fraction of work changes.

cards.question: Bottleneck — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A resource or phase that limits the performance of the current workload.

cards.question: Trust boundary — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A point where data or actions cross between different levels of trust or authority.

cards.question: Valid extent — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The portion of a buffer that the current operation may treat as meaningful input.

cards.question: Mitigation — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A measure that reduces certain consequences or detects certain failures without necessarily preventing the underlying bug.

cards.question: Defense in depth — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Using protections with different coverage so one failed assumption does not remove every defense.

cards.question: Strong exception guarantee — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A promise that a failed operation leaves the relevant observable state unchanged.

cards.question: Durability — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A guarantee about state surviving the failures specified by a storage protocol, distinct from atomic visibility.

cards.question: Translation unit — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A source unit after preprocessing that the compiler processes under the language’s rules.

cards.question: Linking — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Combining compiled definitions and resolving references to build a program or library.

cards.question: Backpressure boundary — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The point at which bounded downstream capacity makes an upstream producer wait or reject work.

cards.question: End-to-end invariant — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A rule spanning several components, such as every accepted input producing exactly one recorded result.
